findings.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:185 — [P1, confidence 100] `work_queue: queue.Queue[WorkItem[T]] = queue.Queue()` creates an unbounded queue, so a slow or blocked per-group processor lets the consumer materialize an unlimited Kafka backlog in RAM until the process is OOM-killed; despite the stated “Natural backpressure” guarantee, no `maxsize` or admission control exists to provide it.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:31 — [P2, confidence 100, advisory] `message: Message[KafkaPayload | FilteredPayload]` retains each raw Kafka message in every queued work item even though no production read of `work_item.message` exists, so a backlog retains both decoded results and raw payloads and raises memory pressure; although offset tracking needs message identity, `partition` and `offset` already supply every field it reads, so deleting `message` removes the redundant retention and all its construction sites.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:238 — [P1, confidence 100] `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` calls the Python 3.13-only `Queue.shutdown` API, so deployments on Python 3.12 or earlier raise `AttributeError` during shutdown and leave every queue worker blocked.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:144 — [confidence 100, P1] The `except Exception:` path logs a failed `self.result_processor(...)` and the unconditional `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` at line 149 marks it successful, so the commit loop permanently advances Kafka past a result whose processing failed.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:233 — [confidence 100, P1] The shutdown sequence `worker.shutdown = True` followed by `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` makes each worker exit after at most its current item instead of draining its queue, so a normal graceful shutdown silently abandons every queued result and leaves their offsets uncommitted for an unbounded duplicate/replay backlog.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:185 — [confidence 100, P1] The unbounded `work_queue: queue.Queue[WorkItem[T]] = queue.Queue()` accepts Kafka messages without a capacity or admission limit when a handler slows or hangs, exhausting consumer memory and terminating the process under sustained backlog.

src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:317 — [confidence 100, P1] The submission `except Exception:` logs a decoder or `grouping_fn` failure and then calls `complete_offset` at lines 320-325, so malformed or newly unsupported messages are committed as successful even though no worker processed them.

tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:1922 — [confidence: 100, severity: P1] The assertion `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` lets the error-path test pass before the one-second commit loop runs, so the worker's `finally: self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` commits the failed message after the test exits while the test falsely validates the advertised no-commit-on-failure guarantee.

tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:1816 — [confidence: 100, severity: P2] The purported concurrency test accepts `if stats["total_items"] == 0 and mock_processor_call.call_count == 2`, so a serial implementation that invokes the mocked processor twice passes and regressions that remove cross-subscription parallelism reach production untested.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:185 — [P1, confidence 100] `work_queue: queue.Queue[WorkItem[T]] = queue.Queue()` creates an unbounded queue, so a slow or blocked per-group processor lets the consumer materialize an unlimited Kafka backlog in RAM until the process is OOM-killed; despite the stated “Natural backpressure” guarantee, no `maxsize` or admission control exists to provide it.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows at line 185 `work_queue: queue.Queue[WorkItem[T]] = queue.Queue()` which creates an unbounded queue with no maxsize parameter. The class docstring at lines 161-168 claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' but this is false since unbounded queues never fill up. If a worker processing a specific group is slow or blocked, messages for that group will accumulate indefinitely in memory. This is a real defect - the code contradicts its documented guarantee and could lead to OOM conditions under load.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:31 — [P2, confidence 100, advisory] `message: Message[KafkaPayload | FilteredPayload]` retains each raw Kafka message in every queued work item even though no production read of `work_item.message` exists, so a backlog retains both decoded results and raw payloads and raises memory pressure; although offset tracking needs message identity, `partition` and `offset` already supply every field it reads, so deleting `message` removes the redundant retention and all its construction sites.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that WorkItem stores the full `message` field (line 31) but this field is never read in the production code - only `partition`, `offset`, and `result` are used. The message is passed through submit() and stored in WorkItem but never accessed afterward. This is a valid memory efficiency concern since queued items retain both the decoded result AND the raw Kafka payload. However, this is not a bug (the code works correctly) but rather a design/efficiency issue. The finding is accurate and actionable - removing the unused `message` field would reduce memory pressure.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:238 — [P1, confidence 100] `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` calls the Python 3.13-only `Queue.shutdown` API, so deployments on Python 3.12 or earlier raise `AttributeError` during shutdown and leave every queue worker blocked.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows line 238 in queue_consumer.py calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` on a `queue.Queue` object. The `Queue.shutdown()` method was only added in Python 3.13 (PEP 661). If this code runs on Python 3.12 or earlier, it will raise `AttributeError: 'Queue' object has no attribute 'shutdown'`. This is a real compatibility bug that would cause the shutdown process to fail on older Python versions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:144 — [confidence 100, P1] The `except Exception:` path logs a failed `self.result_processor(...)` and the unconditional `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` at line 149 marks it successful, so the commit loop permanently advances Kafka past a result whose processing failed.

adjudication.rationale: The finding is accurate. Looking at the diff in queue_consumer.py lines 130-149, the OrderedQueueWorker.run() method has a try/except block where the result_processor is called at line 140. If an exception occurs, it's caught by `except Exception:` at line 144, which only logs the error. However, the `finally:` block at line 147 unconditionally calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` at line 149. This marks the offset as successfully processed even when processing failed, causing the commit loop to advance past failed messages. This is a data loss bug - failed results will be skipped and never reprocessed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:233 — [confidence 100, P1] The shutdown sequence `worker.shutdown = True` followed by `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` makes each worker exit after at most its current item instead of draining its queue, so a normal graceful shutdown silently abandons every queued result and leaves their offsets uncommitted for an unbounded duplicate/replay backlog.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the shutdown sequence in FixedQueuePool.shutdown() (lines 229-238): First it sets worker.shutdown = True for all workers, then calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) on all queues. In OrderedQueueWorker.run() (lines 119-125), the worker loop checks 'while not self.shutdown' and catches queue.ShutDown exception. When shutdown=True is set, the worker will exit after completing its current item (the while loop condition fails). The queue.shutdown(immediate=False) is called after, but by then workers may have already exited due to the shutdown flag being True. This means items remaining in the queues won't be processed, and their offsets won't be marked complete via offset_tracker.complete_offset(), leaving them uncommitted. This is a real bug that could cause data loss/duplicate processing on restart.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:185 — [confidence 100, P1] The unbounded `work_queue: queue.Queue[WorkItem[T]] = queue.Queue()` accepts Kafka messages without a capacity or admission limit when a handler slows or hangs, exhausting consumer memory and terminating the process under sustained backlog.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `queue.Queue()` created at line 185 without any maxsize parameter, making it unbounded. The FixedQueuePool creates these queues and workers submit WorkItems to them via `work_queue.put(work_item)` at line 207. If the result_processor is slow or hangs, messages will accumulate indefinitely in memory since there's no backpressure mechanism. The Kafka consumer will keep submitting messages through SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() which calls queue_pool.submit(), potentially exhausting memory. This is a real defect in a production consumer system.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:317 — [confidence 100, P1] The submission `except Exception:` logs a decoder or `grouping_fn` failure and then calls `complete_offset` at lines 320-325, so malformed or newly unsupported messages are committed as successful even though no worker processed them.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at lines 303-325 in queue_consumer.py, the submit method has a try/except block. When decoder or grouping_fn raises an exception, the except block at line 317 logs the error and then calls add_offset followed by complete_offset (lines 320-325). This marks the offset as successfully processed even though the message was never actually processed by a worker. This means malformed messages or decoder failures will be committed as successful, potentially causing data loss since those messages won't be reprocessed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:1922 — [confidence: 100, severity: P1] The assertion `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` lets the error-path test pass before the one-second commit loop runs, so the worker's `finally: self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` commits the failed message after the test exits while the test falsely validates the advertised no-commit-on-failure guarantee.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a race condition in the test. Looking at the test code at line 1922, it asserts `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` after waiting for processing to complete. However, the `_commit_loop` in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` runs every 1 second (`self.shutdown_event.wait(1.0)`), and the `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` method has `finally: self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` which marks offsets as complete even when exceptions occur. The test waits only 0.2 seconds after processing completes before checking, which may not be enough time for the commit loop to run. More importantly, the worker's finally block unconditionally calls `complete_offset` even on exception, meaning failed messages DO get their offsets marked complete and will eventually be committed - contradicting the test's intended validation that errors prevent commits.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:1816 — [confidence: 100, severity: P2] The purported concurrency test accepts `if stats["total_items"] == 0 and mock_processor_call.call_count == 2`, so a serial implementation that invokes the mocked processor twice passes and regressions that remove cross-subscription parallelism reach production untested.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that test_thread_queue_parallel_concurrent_subscriptions (lines 1760-1800) only verifies that 2 messages were processed and queues are empty, but doesn't actually verify concurrent execution. The test submits messages to different subscriptions and waits for completion, but a serial implementation would also pass this test. However, this is not a bug - it's a test quality issue where the test doesn't adequately verify the concurrency property it claims to test. The test should measure timing or use synchronization primitives to prove concurrent execution.
